prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, showing how reallocation across firms shapes exporting, foreign investment and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed. In round 1 I preferred B019 (Kiyotaki and Moore) and treated B010 as a serious alternative. I now prefer B010 with Helpman and Melitz. The reason is the substance of the exchange, not the number of members on either side. My round-1 objection to B010 was distinctness from the 2008 recognition of new trade theory. The responses answer it. Krugman-style models have symmetric firms, so scale and variety drive the gains. Melitz-style models generate selective exporting, exporter premia, entry and exit, and within-industry reallocation toward more productive firms after liberalisation. These are separate mechanisms with their own testable predictions, and firm-level data have been used to test them in many countries. My own field is growth, firm dynamics and reallocation. From that vantage point, linking firm-level productivity heterogeneity to aggregate productivity and welfare is a conceptual advance, not a refinement of representative-firm trade. It has also spread into macro and growth. Melitz (2003) is the core model, and Helpman, including Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exporting versus FDI, supplies the surrounding architecture, so two names follow the intellectual structure. The framework is over twenty years old, so maturity is not a concern. I would keep the citation narrow, on selection and reallocation. Relative to B019, B010 has the more direct and extensive empirical confirmation, and its credit question is narrower than the Gertler and accelerator boundary. B019 remains a foundational single mechanism with clean two-author credit, and I treat it as the first alternative. My assessments rest on my own recollection of the literature and I have not independently verified them.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is credit. Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum, and Hopenhayn in firm dynamics, are precursors or parallel contributors outside the credited names, and Redding is left out. I would handle this through citation wording and the scientific background, but that is a real cost and not a resolved one. Second, the quantitative gains-from-trade results depend on parametric assumptions such as Pareto productivity draws, so the qualitative mechanism is better established than the size of the welfare gains. Third, trade was recognised in 2008, and the Committee should confirm distinctness on substance and not assume it. I also note that my own earlier uncertainty about distinctness was answered by colleagues' arguments and not by new evidence of my own, so I would not treat my move as independent confirmation. Finally, by moving I give up the single clean mechanism of B019. That mechanism overlaps thematically with the 2022 prize, and its empirical identification is more indirect than its theoretical influence.

responses.point: Hassler argues that heterogeneous-firm trade models differ from new trade theory because they explain which firms export or invest abroad, why aggregate productivity changes after liberalisation, and how reallocation produces welfare gains. He also says Bernard-Jensen motivated the theory but did not supply the unifying model, that Redding is a quantitative and spatial successor, and that the citation should not be a lifetime-achievement one for Helpman.
responses.response: This answers the question I asked in round 1, and it is the main reason I moved. Selection, reallocation and exporter premia are distinct predictions that representative-firm models do not produce, and they have been tested on micro data. I agree on narrow wording and on keeping Redding outside the core pair, since his main contribution builds on the framework. I would qualify one point. The Bernard-Jensen facts did more than motivate the theory, because they set the empirical agenda that the model explains. That is why the scientific background should credit them explicitly, even though the laureate set stays at two. Hassler and I are frequent co-authors and IIES colleagues, so my agreement should not be read as deference.

responses.point: Dreber argues that B010 offers a clear conceptual advance, testable predictions and a long record of confirmation. She grounds distinctness from 2008 in firm-level predictions that could have been rejected. She also names Pareto-dependence of the quantitative claims as her main reservation, and she wants B019's empirical identification discussed explicitly.
responses.response: I agree with both halves. The chair asked whether the qualitative selection and reallocation result survives non-Pareto productivity distributions. From my recollection, the qualitative selection margin and the reallocation toward more productive firms do not depend on Pareto. What is distribution-specific is the clean sufficient-statistic form of the welfare gains and the exact size of the selection channel. So the citation should reward the mechanism and the framework, not a welfare number. That treatment of B010 also lets me answer her B019 point: the evidential gap I accepted for the collateral channel is a real reason to rank B019 second, though I would not call it disqualifying.

responses.point: Strömberg prefers B019 with Kiyotaki and Moore after dropping Gertler. He says the mechanism is a single identifiable discovery with clean credit, that it differs from the 2022 work on banks and runs, and that he is not fully settled on the order of B019 and B010.
responses.response: I share his reading of the mechanism and the two-name boundary, and I still think it is distinct from the 2022 prize in that it concerns collateral values and asset-price feedback and not bank runs. Where we differ is the ranking. Thematic adjacency to 2022 and the weaker direct identification of the amplification channel weigh more for me now. He is also right that the accelerator strand is complementary, not derivative, and I would not oppose adding Gertler if B019 were chosen. If the Committee judges B019 to be clearly distinct from the 2022 work, I would support it as a strong alternative. His own uncertainty about the B019/B010 order suggests we differ in weighting more than in substance.

responses.point: Krusell moved from B037 to B010. He keeps B037 as an alternative only if a defensible boundary for the credit is found, and he raises field balance (trade in 2008, financial crises in 2022, institutions in 2024) as a consideration.
responses.response: I agree that B037 has large policy influence and that its credit is unstable under a three-name limit, since our triads differ. I also think the post-2021 inflation episode should be assessed before treating the baseline as settled. That is why I keep it only as a second alternative. On field balance, I would let it serve at most as a tie-breaker among cases that are comparable on significance, attribution and maturity. I would not let it override the scientific assessment, and on that assessment B010 holds up. Krusell and I are frequent co-authors, so I note that I reached this view through the merits discussed here.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee accepts a two-name citation that omits Redding and the Bernard-Jensen-Eaton-Kortum and Hopenhayn strands, and whether the scientific background can acknowledge them adequately.

How much of the quantitative selection and reallocation gains survives non-Pareto productivity distributions. My view that the qualitative mechanism survives rests on recollection and not on checked sources.
Whether B010 is judged a distinct advance beyond the 2008 trade prize. I am now persuaded, but others may weigh field balance differently.

Whether B019 should be preferred if the Committee finds the 2022 overlap not decisive and values a single clean mechanism over a larger body of confirming evidence, and whether Gertler would then be added.
Whether my move reflects independent reassessment or too much deference to the convergence of colleagues' views. I have tried to base it on the substantive arguments about distinctness and evidence.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Helpman, Melitz or Redding appears in my supplied profile, and none to the B019 candidates (Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler, Gilchrist). Disclosed for transparency: my research on firm dynamics, reallocation and creative destruction is field-proximate to B010. I have a long-running collaboration with Philippe Aghion, Antonin Bergeaud, Peter Klenow and Huiyu Li, and Klenow is credited on B013, which I do not propose. I am a frequent co-author and IIES colleague of Per Krusell (secretary) and John Hassler (chair), both of whom prefer B010. My profile also lists Michael Peters, Fabrizio Zilibotti and others as co-authors, and none of them is credited on any entry I propose. These ties are disclosed and not adjudicated.
